mean: happy to give money, time or help to others
ex: Our generous landlord in Hyderabad let Salim skip two months' rent when he lost his job.
note: It also means large: 'a generous helping of biryani'. Generous is about giving; kind is wider.
ex2: At the Durga Puja pandal, a generous shopkeeper quietly paid for the bhog served to the whole lane.

mean: caring only about yourself and not about others
ex: It was selfish of Varun to finish the hostel's shared stock of Maggi without telling anyone.
note: Selfish is about actions that cost others; 'self-centred' is about always thinking and talking about yourself.
ex2: On the Mumbai local, a selfish passenger kept his bag on the seat while an old man stood beside him.

mean: can be trusted to do what is needed, every time
ex: Bhaskar is the most reliable person on the team; if he says Friday, the report comes on Friday.
note: Used for people, machines and information alike. 'Dependable' is a close synonym.
ex2: Our old Maruti is not fast, but it is reliable and has never broken down on the road to Manali.

mean: able to wait or deal with problems calmly, without getting angry
ex: The patient teacher explained long division to Gauri for the fourth time, still smiling.
note: Same spelling as the noun 'patient' (a sick person). The quality is 'patience', not 'patients'. Opposite: impatient.
ex2: The patient farmer in Ratnagiri waited four years for his mango saplings to bear their first fruit.

mean: refusing to change your mind, even when you should
ex: My stubborn grandfather refuses to use Google Maps and still asks every paanwala for directions.
note: Usually negative. The praising words for the same quality are 'determined' or 'tenacious'.
ex2: The stubborn opener blocked ball after ball on the final day until the bowlers were exhausted.

mean: not proud; not thinking you are better than others
ex: Despite his national award, the humble scientist still takes the Delhi metro to his lab every day.
note: 'Humble beginnings' means born poor. Avoid 'I humbly request' in every email; it sounds old-fashioned.
ex2: Even after topping the state board exams, Lakshmi stayed humble and thanked her tuition teacher first.

mean: acting as if you are better or more important than others
ex: The arrogant new manager ignored advice from dock workers who had run the Kochi port for decades.
note: 'Proud' can be good (proud of my daughter); arrogant never is. Noun: arrogance.
ex2: The arrogant batsman waved to the crowd before reaching his century and was bowled the very next ball.

mean: honest and really meaning what you say or feel
ex: Ayesha's apology was sincere; she came to the shop herself instead of just sending a text.
note: Sincere is about true feelings; honest is about true facts. 'Yours sincerely' ends a letter to a named person.
ex2: Rohan made a sincere effort to learn Tamil after moving to Chennai, practising with his neighbours every evening.

mean: having a strong wish to succeed or achieve big things
ex: Ambitious young Mohit sells vada pav by day and studies for the civil services exam at night.
note: Praise for a person's drive; for a plan it can hint 'maybe too big', as in 'an ambitious deadline'.
ex2: The city's ambitious plan to build fifty new parks in two years got a cautious welcome from residents.

mean: careful to avoid risks or danger
ex: Being cautious, Uncle Thomas reads every line of a loan form before he signs anything.
note: 'Cautiously optimistic' (hopeful but careful) is common in news. Cautious is wise care; timid is fear.
ex2: After the floods, the cooperative bank was cautious about giving new loans to farmers in the district.

mean: doing things suddenly, without thinking first
ex: In an impulsive moment during a midnight online sale, Riya bought three phones she didn't need.
note: Impulsive acts on sudden urges, often with regret; 'spontaneous' is the friendlier word for unplanned fun.
ex2: An impulsive shot in the last over cost the team the match and the series.

mean: working carefully and steadily, putting real effort into every task
ex: The diligent clerk at the tehsil office kept every land record neatly filed and up to date.
note: Diligent adds care and steadiness, not just long hours. 'Due diligence' means careful checking before a deal.
ex2: Meena is a diligent gardener who waters her tulsi and chilli plants before dawn every single day.

mean: honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable
ex: In a candid interview, the retired umpire admitted he had made mistakes in some big matches.
note: A 'candid photo' is taken without posing. Candid means frank, but not rude.
ex2: Over chai, my grandmother was candid: she had married at sixteen and wished she had studied further.

mean: very careful about every small detail
ex: The meticulous tailor in Chandni Chowk measured Kabir three times before cutting the sherwani cloth.
note: Stronger than 'careful' and mostly praise. Taken too far, it becomes 'fussy' or 'nitpicking'.
ex2: Meticulous planning by the wedding caterer meant five hundred guests were served dinner in under an hour.

mean: able to recover quickly after trouble or hardship
ex: The resilient fishing families of Puri rebuilt their boats within weeks of the cyclone.
note: Resilient is about bouncing back after a blow; tenacious is about not letting go during the fight.
ex2: Mumbai is a resilient city; the morning after the heaviest rain, the local trains were packed again.

mean: dealing with problems in a practical, sensible way rather than by ideals
ex: Instead of waiting for a new building, the pragmatic headmistress held classes under the banyan tree.
note: Pragmatic can hint that ideals were set aside to get results. The form is 'pragmatic', never 'pragmatical'.
ex2: Being pragmatic, Arjun took the steady bank job first and kept writing his novel on weekends.

mean: careful to say things in a way that does not upset people
ex: When the groom's aunt criticised the food, the tactful caterer simply offered her more rasmalai.
note: Opposite: tactless. Tactful is about sparing feelings, not hiding the truth; 'diplomatic' is a close synonym.
ex2: Asked whether she liked her mother-in-law's cooking, the tactful bride said the dal was her favourite dish.

mean: believing people act only for selfish reasons
ex: After years of broken promises about the new road, the villagers had become cynical about every announcement.
note: Cynical doubts motives ('they only want something'); sceptical doubts claims until there is proof. Sceptical is the healthier habit.
ex2: Some viewers have grown cynical about TV debates where everyone shouts and nobody listens.

mean: easily tricked because you believe whatever you are told
ex: A gullible uncle in the family WhatsApp group forwarded the fake lottery message to all fifty members.
note: Stronger than 'naive': naive means lacking experience; gullible means actually getting fooled.
ex2: Gullible tourists at the railway station paid five hundred rupees for a two-kilometre auto ride.

mean: talking to people as if they are less clever or important than you
ex: The condescending salesman explained the phone very slowly to Ammini, unaware she was a retired engineer.
note: Close to 'patronising'. Arrogant is how you see yourself; condescending is how you treat others.
ex2: The senior doctor's condescending tone made the young nurse afraid to ask any more questions.

mean: distant and cool; keeping away from other people
ex: The new boy seemed aloof at first, but Nikhil soon learnt he was just shy and new to Kolkata.
note: What looks aloof is often shyness. 'Stand aloof from' means to deliberately stay out of something.
ex2: The star cricketer stayed aloof from the reporters, walking straight past them to the team bus.

mean: very serious and sincere about what you are doing
ex: The earnest young volunteer spent every Sunday teaching children in the basti to read and write.
note: 'In earnest' means seriously, for real: 'The monsoon began in earnest in July.' Sometimes earnest hints 'a bit too serious'.
ex2: Jatin made an earnest request to the principal to keep the school library open on Sundays.

mean: refusing to give up; holding on firmly to a goal
ex: The tenacious RTI applicant filed appeal after appeal until the ration shop records were made public.
note: Praise for persistence; 'stubborn' is its negative cousin. Noun: tenacity.
ex2: The tenacious goalkeeper from Manipur saved three penalties in the final shootout.

mean: someone who flatters powerful people to get favours
ex: Every office has a sycophant who laughs loudest at the boss's jokes and agrees before he finishes.
note: This is the English word for a 'chamcha'. Adjective: sycophantic. Stress the first syllable: SIK-uh-funt.
ex2: At the film party, a sycophant kept praising the director's weakest film as a masterpiece.

mean: generous and kind, especially towards a rival or someone who hurt you
ex: In a magnanimous speech, the new sarpanch thanked her defeated rival and invited him onto the water committee.
note: Not generosity with money but generosity of spirit, usually towards an opponent. 'Magnanimous in victory' is the classic phrase.
ex2: The champion was magnanimous in victory, raising her young rival's hand before the cheering Pune crowd.

mean: acting morally better than others in a smug, preachy way
ex: Our sanctimonious neighbour lectures everyone about saving water, then washes his car with a hose every morning.
note: Like 'holier-than-thou', or someone always giving 'gyaan'. Always an insult; it has nothing to do with real holiness.
ex2: The sanctimonious uncle lectured the cousins about screen time while scrolling reels at the dinner table.

mean: sure of yourself and what you can do
ex: After months of practice, Tanvi felt confident enough to speak in English at the college debate.
note: Confident (sure of yourself) is not confidant (a person you trust with secrets).
ex2: The confident young shopkeeper in Shillong explained every phone model to customers without once checking the box.

mean: not willing to work or make an effort
ex: The lazy contractor left the pothole half-filled and never came back before the monsoon.
note: Calling a colleague lazy is blunt; at work, 'not very motivated' sounds kinder.
ex2: After the big Diwali lunch, everyone felt too lazy to help Nani with the dishes.

mean: not polite; showing no respect for others
ex: The rude ticket checker shouted at an old woman who could not find her ticket fast enough.
note: Rude is about bad manners; crude means vulgar or rough.
ex2: It is rude to take a phone call in the middle of a job interview.

mean: always supporting a person, group or team
ex: Kolkata's football fans are fiercely loyal; they fill the stadium even when their club keeps losing.
note: Say 'loyal to someone', not 'loyal for someone'.
ex2: Shankar has been a loyal customer of the same Udupi hotel in Matunga for thirty years.

mean: not talking much about your own skills or success
ex: The modest batter said the century belonged to the groundsmen who had prepared the pitch.
note: Modest can also mean small or simple: 'a modest salary', 'a modest house'.
ex2: Though her catering business in Lucknow is a big success, Zoya is modest and calls it 'just a small kitchen'.

mean: saying exactly what you think, even if others dislike it
ex: The outspoken nurse told the hospital board that the night shift had far too few staff.
note: Usually praise. Blunt and tactless are the ruder cousins.
ex2: My outspoken aunt told the matchmaker she cared about the boy's kindness, not his salary.

mean: having good judgment; practical and wise
ex: Sensible families in Chennai pack an emergency kit well before the cyclone season.
note: Trap: sensible means wise, not sensitive. A sensitive person feels things deeply.
ex2: Ravi is the sensible one in our hostel group; he always keeps money aside for the bus home.

mean: saying clearly and confidently what you need or think, without being rude
ex: Shreya learnt to be assertive and finally told her manager she could not take on a fourth project.
note: Assertive is firm and respectful; aggressive is pushy and hostile.
ex2: The assertive passenger politely but firmly asked the man to stop smoking on the platform.

mean: able to understand and share other people's feelings
ex: The empathetic doctor sat with the worried family and explained the scan in simple Marathi.
note: Empathy is feeling WITH someone; sympathy is feeling sorry FOR them.
ex2: An empathetic teacher noticed Imran had gone quiet after moving schools and stayed back to talk to him.

mean: strange or unusual in a harmless, often amusing way
ex: The eccentric professor cycled across the campus in a raincoat even in the dry heat of May.
note: Eccentric is gentle, even fond; 'weird' or 'mad' can sound rude.
ex2: Our eccentric neighbour in Goa has named each of his twelve cats after a famous footballer.

mean: too trusting because you have little experience of life
ex: It was naive of Anil to think his first startup would make money in six months.
note: Say nye-EEV, not 'nev'. Milder than gullible: it is about inexperience.
ex2: The naive tourist believed the guide who claimed the Taj Mahal was built in a single year.

mean: trying to seem more important, clever or classy than you are
ex: The pretentious café in Bandra called plain toast 'artisanal bread with rustic butter' and charged four hundred rupees.
note: Pretentious is putting on airs; arrogant is looking down on others.
ex2: Ishaan's pretentious habit of quoting French writers at family dinners made his cousins roll their eyes.

mean: quiet and simple; not trying to get attention
ex: The unassuming man who ran the photocopy shop turned out to be a state chess champion.
note: A warm, positive word, close to humble but about manner and looks.
ex2: Despite her Olympic medal, the unassuming wrestler went back to her Haryana village by bus.

mean: rough and harsh in a way that upsets people
ex: The new editor was brilliant but abrasive, and three reporters asked for transfers within a month.
note: Literally abrasive means rough enough to scrape, like sandpaper.
ex2: His abrasive comments in the housing society WhatsApp group made even friendly neighbours stop replying.

mean: very fussy about small details or cleanliness; hard to please
ex: My fastidious mother-in-law wipes every steel glass twice before she gives a guest water.
note: Close to meticulous, but fastidious hints at being fussy and hard to please.
ex2: The fastidious editor sent the report back three times because of commas in the wrong places.

mean: changing mood or mind suddenly and often
ex: The mercurial fast bowler could take five wickets one day and leak fifty runs the next.
note: Often used of gifted but unpredictable sportspeople and artists.
ex2: Working for a mercurial boss in Gurugram, Sunita never knew if a meeting would bring praise or shouting.
